arXiv:1505.07500v1 [math.AP] 27 May 2015

Stability of the solitary wave solutions to a coupled BBM system

Hongqiu Chen and Xiao-Jun Wang* Email address: hchen1@memphis.edu Email address: xwang13@memphis.edu
Abstract.

In this work, we present a stability criteria for the solitary wave solutions to a BBM system that contains coupled nonlinear terms. Using the idea by Bona, Chen and Karakashian [5] and exploiting the accurate point spectrum information of the associated Schro¨\ddot{o}dinger operator, we improve the stability results previously got by Pereira [15].

Hongqiu Chen

Department of mathematical sciences, University of Memphis, TN, 38152

Xiao-Jun Wang

Department of mathematical sciences, University of Memphis, TN, 38152

1. Introduction

This work is essentially motivated by two papers, [5] and [15]. In [5], Bona, Chen and Karakashian consider a class of BBM-type systems in form of

ut+ux−ux​x​t+P​(u,v)x=0,\displaystyle u_{t}+u_{x}-u_{xxt}+P(u,v)_{x}=0,
(1) vt+vx−vx​x​t+Q​(u,v)x=0,\displaystyle v_{t}+v_{x}-v_{xxt}+Q(u,v)_{x}=0,

where

P⁡(u,v)=A​u2+B​u​v+C​v2,Q⁡(u,v)=D​u2+E​u​v+F​v2P(u,v)=Au^{2}+Buv+Cv^{2},\quad Q(u,v)=Du^{2}+Euv+Fv^{2}

with constants A,B,⋯,F∈ℝA,B,\cdots,F\in\mathbb{R}. Namely, PP and QQ are homogeneous, quadratic polynomials. The other paper [15] by Pereira considers BBM system

(2) Ut+c0​Ux−A​Ux​x​t+(∇H​(u))x=0,\displaystyle U_{t}+c_{0}U_{x}-AU_{xxt}+(\nabla H(u))_{x}=0,

where U=U⁡(x,t)U=U(x,t) is an ℛ2\mathcal{R}^{2}-valued function, c0c_{0} is a non-negative parameter, AA is a 2×22\times 2 real positive definite matrix, and ∇H\nabla H is the gradient of a homogeneous function H:ℛ2→ℛH:\mathcal{R}^{2}\rightarrow\mathcal{R} with proper regularity. The nonlinear terms in (2) can be seen as generalizations of that in (1), since the latter were essentially forced into a structure of the same form as the former, due to certain positiveness requirement. However, the result in [5] turns out to be stronger than that in [15]. The reason is that, in a proper space, [5] takes into account the accurate point spectrum information of the Schro¨\ddot{o}dinger operator ℒ0=−d2d​x2−ϕ⁡(x)\mathcal{L}_{0}=-{d^{2}\over dx^{2}}-\phi(x), where ϕ\phi is a typical potential function. Here we present a stability result which generalizes [5] and improves [15].

1.1. Main result

We consider a BBM system in form of

(3) Ut+Ux−Ux​x​t+(∇H​(U))x=0,\displaystyle U_{t}+U_{x}-U_{xxt}+(\nabla H(U))_{x}=0,

where U=U⁡(x,t)U=U(x,t) is an ℛ2\mathcal{R}^{2} valued function and ∇H=(Hu,Hv)t\nabla H=(H_{u},H_{v})^{t} is the gradient of a C3C^{3} homogeneous function H:ℛ2→ℛH:\mathcal{R}^{2}\rightarrow\mathcal{R}, the superscript t represents transpose. The equations are the same as in (2), except that we have simplified the system by letting c0=1c_{0}=1 and A=I2×2A=I_{2\times 2} for sake of clarity. The techniques used in this work apply to cases with more general c0c_{0} or AA. In this note we focus on the stability results. We refer to [9, 14] for global well-posedness of (3), or [15, 9] for instability results.

The functional space is L2​(ℛ)L^{2}(\mathcal{R}), in which the scalar operator ℒ\mathcal{L} defined below has domain H2​(ℛ)H^{2}(\mathcal{R}). While in the coupled system, the natural product spaces L2​(ℛ)×L2​(ℛ)L^{2}(\mathcal{R})\times L^{2}(\mathcal{R}) and H2​(ℛ)×H2​(ℛ)H^{2}(\mathcal{R})\times H^{2}(\mathcal{R}) are used. The operator ℒ\mathcal{L} sends H1​(ℛ)H^{1}(\mathcal{R}) to H−1​(ℛ)H^{-1}(\mathcal{R}); <ℒ​u,u><\mathcal{L}u,u> denotes the the pairing of ℒ​u\mathcal{L}u and uu on space H−1​(ℛ)H^{-1}(\mathcal{R}) and H1​(ℛ)H^{1}(\mathcal{R}). We shall not further dig into the issues on space setting, instead we simply assume all the functions here have enough regularity for all the operations under consideration. However, precise functional settings are crucial in both the well-posedness and the stability proofs, for instance, in case of the space decomposition [6].

We assume here the homogeneous function H⁡(⋅,⋅)H(\cdot,\cdot) is of order p+2p+2 with integer p≥1p\geq 1. Suppose Φ=(ϕ,μ​ϕ)t\Phi=(\phi,\mu\phi)^{t} is a proportional solitary wave solution of (3), where μ∈ℛ\mu\in\mathcal{R} is the proportional coefficient. Assume Hu​(1,μ)>0H_{u}(1,\mu)>0 and let

ℳ=1(p+1)​Hu​(1,μ)​(Hu​u​(1,μ)Hu​v​(1,μ)Hu​v​(1,μ)Hv​v​(1,μ)).\mathcal{M}={1\over(p+1)H_{u}(1,\mu)}\left(\begin{array}[]{cc}H_{uu}(1,\mu)&H_{uv}(1,\mu)\\ H_{uv}(1,\mu)&H_{vv}(1,\mu)\end{array}\right).

Our main result is

Theorem 1.1.

Assume det(ℳ)<1p+1\det(\mathcal{M})<{1\over p+1}. We have

  1. (1)

    for p≤4p\leq 4, Φ\Phi is stable;

  2. (2)

    if p>4p>4, then there exists a ωp>1\omega_{p}>1 such that Φ\Phi is stable for ω>ωp\omega>\omega_{p} and unstable for 1<ω<ωp1<\omega<\omega_{p}.

Remark 1.2.

Secret-telling moments.

  1. (1)

    In this note, we only consider the proportional solitary wave solution. Nevertheless, as the study of nonlinear Schro¨\ddot{o}dinger system suggests [19], non-proportional solitary wave solutions do exist and are of great importance in real applications.

  2. (2)

    Given HH, one can easily compute det(ℳ)\det(\mathcal{M}) and determine the stability of a solitary wave. This idea was first brought up in [5]. The accurate information on eigenvalues is the key to discover the condition under which the stability is achieved.

1.2. Strategy

Since Benjamin [3] set up the rigid mathematical framework, with refinements, generalization and elaboration along the way [4, 16, 17, 18, 8, 2, 6, 13] etc., stability study in this direction has developed into a sophisticate but “routine” process. On the one hand, it has close relations with areas such as scattering/inverse scattering theory, spectrum theory, hamiltonian systems, etc., see [12]; on the other hand, the classical method more or less follows a routine process in proving the stability of a solitary wave solution, ϕ\phi for instance:

  • •

    formulate the proper metric ||⋅||||\cdot|| to measure the shape deviation;

  • •

    capture a pair of conserved quantities to form a Lyapunov functional LL, which is invariant too;

  • •

    for any solution uu with perturbation v=u−ϕv=u-\phi, investigate L⁡(u)−L⁡(ϕ)L(u)-L(\phi) and show there exist positive constants C1,C2C_{1},C_{2} such that for all time,

    (4) C1​‖v‖2+o⁡(‖v‖2)≤L⁡(u)−L⁡(ϕ)≤C2​‖v‖2+o⁡(‖v‖2).C_{1}||v||^{2}+o(||v||^{2})\leq L(u)-L(\phi)\leq C_{2}||v||^{2}+o(||v||^{2}).

Then the second inequality at time t=0t=0 implies that L⁡(u)−L⁡(ϕ)L(u)-L(\phi) is bounded by initial deviation OPEN‖v⁡(0)‖2=‖u⁡(0)−ϕ‖2)||v(0)||^{2}=||u(0)-\phi||^{2}), at least when vv is small; the first inequality at all later time implies all deviations ‖v‖2||v||^{2} are bounded by L⁡(u)−L⁡(ϕ)L(u)-L(\phi). The fact that L⁡(u)−L⁡(ϕ)L(u)-L(\phi) is invariant gives the stability: the initial deviation (shape difference) bounds the future deviation, at least when the initial deviation is small.

This clear picture does not show up without subtle issues. The global well-posedness needs to be ready; the key player-a solitary wave solution has to exist; to maintain an effective norm, the infimum of the deviation has to happen within a finite translation[4]; how to transfer a constrained result to a general one, etc. But the most delicate part is the establishment of inequality (4).

In estimating L⁡(u)−L⁡(ϕ)L(u)-L(\phi), a self-adjoint operator ℒ\mathcal{L} shows up. Roughly, we have L⁡(u)−L⁡(ϕ)=<ℒ​v,v>+o⁡(‖v‖2)L(u)-L(\phi)=<\mathcal{L}v,v>+o(||v||^{2}), where <⋅,⋅><\cdot,\cdot> denotes the adjoint pair on H−1​(ℛ)×H1​(ℛ)H^{-1}(\mathcal{R})\times H^{1}(\mathcal{R}). The upper bound, L⁡(u)−L⁡(ϕ)≤C2​‖v‖2+o⁡(‖v‖2)L(u)-L(\phi)\leq C_{2}||v||^{2}+o(||v||^{2}), is easy to show, since ℒ\mathcal{L} is bounded operator from H1​(ℛ)H^{1}(\mathcal{R}) to H−1​(ℛ)H^{-1}(\mathcal{R}). The lower bound requires certain amount of “positiveness” of ℒ\mathcal{L}. The operator is generally not positive definite, but almost so: the residual spectrum is missing since the operator is self-adjoint; it has strictly positive continuous spectrum; it has a simple zero eigenvalue and a unique, simple, negative eigenvalue. Thus, the space under investigation is able to be decomposed into a direct product of certain subspaces and the major part of the positiveness is kept, so is the positiveness of the lower order term ‖v‖2||v||^{2}.

This classical method calls for a pack of techniques that attach to the analysis of such an operator. To avoid these difficulties, the concentration-compactness method has been developed by Cazenave and Lions from the calculus of variation viewpoint, see [7, 11].

We shall embrace the tradition and follow the process mentioned above. But as has been remarked before, we shall omit some “critical but routine” steps and focus on the those parts which reflect the improvements we provide: the accurate spectrum analysis on the Schro¨\ddot{o}dinger operator; the calculation of a critical quantity d′′​(ω)d^{\prime\prime}(\omega). Some examples are given in the end.

1.3. Preliminaries

1.3.1. Point spectrum of Schro¨\ddot{o}dinger operator

The result in this work relies on the precise information on the point spectrum of a specific Schro¨\ddot{o}dinger operator, ℒ0=−Δ+V⁡(x)\mathcal{L}_{0}=-\Delta+V(x) in one dimensional space, where the Laplacian Δ=d2d​x2\Delta={d^{2}\over dx^{2}} and VV is a potential function. In the special case where the potential function V⁡(x)=−α​sech2​(x),α>0V(x)=-\alpha\mbox{sech}^{2}(x),\alpha>0, the eigenvalue problem can be solved explicitly; see Landau etal. [10], page 73-74. Here for sake of completeness, we reproduce some details in this aspect.

On space L2​(ℛ)L^{2}(\mathcal{R}), this ϕ⁡(x)\phi(x) make ℒ0\mathcal{L}_{0} a self-adjoint operator. Let σ\sigma denote the full spectrum and let σp,σc,σr\sigma_{p},\sigma_{c},\sigma_{r} be the point spectrum, the continuous spectrum and residual spectrum, respectively. For self-adjoint operator the residual spectrum is missing, we have σ⁡(ℒ0)=σp​(ℒ0)∪σc​(ℒ0)\sigma(\mathcal{L}_{0})=\sigma_{p}(\mathcal{L}_{0})\cup\sigma_{c}(\mathcal{L}_{0}). Moreover,

Lemma 1.3.

[Pava [12]] we have

  1. (1)

    −d2d​x2-{d^{2}\over dx^{2}} has spectrum σ=σc=[0,∞)\sigma=\sigma_{c}=[0,\infty).

  2. (2)

    −d2d​x2+ω-{d^{2}\over dx^{2}}+\omega has spectrum σ=σc=[ω,∞)\sigma=\sigma_{c}=[\omega,\infty).

  3. (3)

    ℒ0=−d2d​x2+ω−α​sech2​(x)\mathcal{L}_{0}=-{d^{2}\over dx^{2}}+\omega-\alpha\mbox{sech}^{2}(x), being self-adjoint on L2​(ℛ)L^{2}(\mathcal{R}), has only real spectrum, which consists of the continuous part [ω,∞)[\omega,\infty), together with a finite number of discrete eigenvalues in (−∞,ω)(-\infty,\omega).

To find the eigenvalues of ℒ0\mathcal{L}_{0}, we shall solve

ψ~​(ξ)→0, as ​ξ→±1.\tilde{\psi}(\xi)\rightarrow 0,\mbox{ as }\xi\rightarrow\pm 1.

Lemma 1.4 (Theorem B.61,[12]).

Suppose that ϕ∈L2​(ℛ)\phi\in L^{2}(\mathcal{R}) satisfies the differential equation

−ϕ′′+c​ϕ−f⁡(ϕ)=0,-\phi^{\prime\prime}+c\phi-f(\phi)=0,

defined in L2​(ℛ)L^{2}(\mathcal{R}) has exactly one simple negative eigenvalue λ0\lambda_{0}; the eigenvalue 00 is simple with associated eigenfunction ϕ′\phi^{\prime}; and there exists δ>0\delta>0 such that every λ∈σ⁡(L0)−{λ0,0}\lambda\in\sigma(L_{0})-\{\lambda_{0},0\} satisfies λ>δ\lambda>\delta.

1.3.2. Scalar equation

In this part, by comparing with the scalar equation, we single out the difficulties brought up by the coupling mechanism and focus on these new issues.

Consider a scalar BBM equation

(12) ut+ux−ux​x​t+ℏ​up​ux=0,u_{t}+u_{x}-u_{xxt}+\hbar u^{p}u_{x}=0,

We assume the solitary wave solution exists in form of ϕω​(x−ω​t)\phi_{\omega}(x-\omega t). Then let z=x−ω​t,ϕ⁡(z)=ϕω​(x−ω​t)z=x-\omega t,\phi(z)=\phi_{\omega}(x-\omega t), substitute into (12), we have

has eigenfunction ϕ′\phi^{\prime} corresponding to eigenvalue 00.

Let

d⁡(ω)=Θ0​(ϕω)+ω​Ω0​(ϕω).d(\omega)=\Theta_{0}(\phi_{\omega})+\omega\Omega_{0}(\phi_{\omega}).

The classical result is, the main inequality (4) will be established if

holds, however, under the constraint

Remark 1.5.

For a general solitary wave solution, there is a requirement on the existence of an interval of ω\omega, on which d⁡(ω)d(\omega) has certain smoothness. It is not a problem for the special solitary solution ϕ\phi here.

Four the coupled system (3), we shall walk through the same procedure, however, with conserved quantities and operator in different forms. And the main difficulty comes from the spectrum analysis of the new operator.

1.3.3. Coupled system

Consider (3),

Ut+Ux−Ux​x​t+(∇H​(U))x=0,U_{t}+U_{x}-U_{xxt}+(\nabla H(U))_{x}=0,

We have conserved quantities

Ω⁡(U)=12​∫ℛUt​U+Uxt​Ux​𝑑x,\Omega(U)={1\over 2}\int_{\mathcal{R}}U^{t}U+U_{x}^{t}U_{x}dx,
Θ(U)=−12∫ℛUtU+2H(U)dx.\Theta(U)=-{1\over 2}\int_{\mathcal{R}}U^{t}U+2H(U)dx.

We consider the proportional solitary wave solution U⁡(x,t)=Φω​(x−ω​t)=(ϕω​(x−ω​t),ψω​(x−ω​t))tU(x,t)=\Phi_{\omega}(x-\omega t)=(\phi_{\omega}(x-\omega t),\psi_{\omega}(x-\omega t))^{t} of system (3), where ψω=μ​ϕω\psi_{\omega}=\mu\phi_{\omega} with μ\mu a real constant. Later on, we often write ϕ,ψ\phi,\psi for ϕω​(x−ω​t),ψω​(x−ω​t)\phi_{\omega}(x-\omega t),\psi_{\omega}(x-\omega t) when it is in a clear context.

Hv​(1,μ)=μ​Hu​(1,μ),H_{v}(1,\mu)=\mu H_{u}(1,\mu),

and

(15) −ω​ϕ′′+(ω−1)​ϕ−Hu​(1,μ)​ϕp+1=0.-\omega\phi^{\prime\prime}+(\omega-1)\phi-H_{u}(1,\mu)\phi^{p+1}=0.

ℳ=1(p+1)​Hu​(1,μ)​(Hu​u​(1,μ)Hu​v​(1,μ)Hu​v​(1,μ)Hv​v​(1,μ))\mathcal{M}={1\over(p+1)H_{u}(1,\mu)}\left(\begin{array}[]{cc}H_{uu}(1,\mu)&H_{uv}(1,\mu)\\ H_{uv}(1,\mu)&H_{vv}(1,\mu)\end{array}\right)
=1b1+(p+2)​b2​(b1+p​b22​b22​b2b1+p​b2).={1\over b_{1}+(p+2)b_{2}}\left(\begin{array}[]{cc}b_{1}+pb_{2}&2b_{2}\\ 2b_{2}&b_{1}+pb_{2}\end{array}\right).
det(ℳ)<1p+1⇒(p+1)​[(b1+p​b2)2−4​b22]<(b1+(p+2)​b2)2\det(\mathcal{M})<{1\over p+1}\Rightarrow(p+1)[(b_{1}+pb_{2})^{2}-4b_{2}^{2}]<(b_{1}+(p+2)b_{2})^{2}
⇒(p+1)[(b1+(p−2)b2][(b1+(p+2)b2]<(b1+(p+2)b2)2\Rightarrow(p+1)[(b_{1}+(p-2)b_{2}][(b_{1}+(p+2)b_{2}]<(b_{1}+(p+2)b_{2})^{2}
⇒(p+1)[(b1+(p−2)b2]<(b1+(p+2)b2)\Rightarrow(p+1)[(b_{1}+(p-2)b_{2}]<(b_{1}+(p+2)b_{2})
⇒p​b1≤−(p+1)​(p−3)​b2\Rightarrow pb_{1}\leq-(p+1)(p-3)b_{2}
⇒b1≤−(p+1)​(p−3)p​b2.\Rightarrow b_{1}\leq-{(p+1)(p-3)\over p}b_{2}.

To get the third inequality from bottom, the assumption Hu=b1+(p+2)​b2>0H_{u}=b_{1}+(p+2)b_{2}>0 is used, which gives a lower bound for b1b_{1}, same as (18) and (19). To see that our result is stronger, first note that b2>0b_{2}>0 holds true by comparing the first and third terms in inequality (18) (or (19)). Then, it is easy to verify that the upper bounds given here are larger than those given in (18) and (19).

Example 4.2.

Let q≥1q\geq 1 be an integer. Consider

ut+ux−ux​x​t+(uq​vq+1)x=0,u_{t}+u_{x}-u_{xxt}+(u^{q}v^{q+1})_{x}=0,
vt+vx−vx​x​t+(uq+1​vq)x=0.v_{t}+v_{x}-v_{xxt}+(u^{q+1}v^{q})_{x}=0.

This is an example considered in [9], where the result (Lemma 3.1) requires ω−1+Hu​v−Hu2>0\omega-1+H_{uv}-H_{u^{2}}>0, which is obviously a much stronger assumption than ours. This is exactly the point: by taking advantage of the accurate point spectrum information, we weaken conditions like this.

By our result

H⁡(u,v)=uq+1​vq+1q+1.H(u,v)={u^{q+1}v^{q+1}\over q+1}.

Existence of solitary wave solution forces μ=1\mu=1. This case corresponds to p=2​q−1p=2q-1. We have here

ℳ=1(p+1)​Hu​(1,μ)​(Hu​u​(1,μ)Hu​v​(1,μ)Hu​v​(1,μ)Hv​v​(1,μ))\mathcal{M}={1\over(p+1)H_{u}(1,\mu)}\left(\begin{array}[]{cc}H_{uu}(1,\mu)&H_{uv}(1,\mu)\\ H_{uv}(1,\mu)&H_{vv}(1,\mu)\end{array}\right)
=12​q2​(q⁡(q−1)q⁡(q+1)q⁡(q+1)q⁡(q−1)).={1\over 2q^{2}}\left(\begin{array}[]{cc}q(q-1)&q(q+1)\\ q(q+1)&q(q-1)\end{array}\right).

Hence

det(ℳ)=−1q<0<1p+1=12​q.\det(\mathcal{M})=-{1\over q}<0<{1\over p+1}={1\over 2q}.

The condition is satisfied, so Theorem 1.1 applies.

Example 4.3.

Let q≥1q\geq 1 be an integer. Let A,B≠0A,B\neq 0, consider the decoupled system

ut+ux−ux​x​t+(A​up+1)x=0,u_{t}+u_{x}-u_{xxt}+(Au^{p+1})_{x}=0,
vt+vx−vx​x​t+(B​vp+1)x=0.v_{t}+v_{x}-v_{xxt}+(Bv^{p+1})_{x}=0.

In this case

H⁡(u,v)=A​up+2+B​vp+2q+2.H(u,v)={Au^{p+2}+Bv^{p+2}\over q+2}.
Hv​(1,μ)=μ​Hu​(1,μ)⇒B​μp+1=A​μH_{v}(1,\mu)=\mu H_{u}(1,\mu)\Rightarrow B\mu^{p+1}=A\mu
⇒μ=0, or ​B​μp=A.\Rightarrow\mu=0,\mbox{ or }B\mu^{p}=A.
ℳ=1(p+1)​Hu​(1,μ)​(Hu​u​(1,μ)Hu​v​(1,μ)Hu​v​(1,μ)Hv​v​(1,μ))\mathcal{M}={1\over(p+1)H_{u}(1,\mu)}\left(\begin{array}[]{cc}H_{uu}(1,\mu)&H_{uv}(1,\mu)\\ H_{uv}(1,\mu)&H_{vv}(1,\mu)\end{array}\right)
=1(p+1)​A​(A⁡(p+1)00B⁡(p+1)​μp).={1\over(p+1)A}\left(\begin{array}[]{cc}A(p+1)&0\\ 0&B(p+1)\mu^{p}\end{array}\right).

Hence

det(ℳ)=B​μpA.\det(\mathcal{M})={B\mu^{p}\over A}.

If μ=0\mu=0, then det(ℳ)=0<1p+1\det(\mathcal{M})=0<{1\over p+1}. Theorem 1.1 applies.
If μ≠0\mu\neq 0, then det(ℳ)=1>1p+1\det(\mathcal{M})=1>{1\over p+1}.

This is a slight generalization of example in [5]. It tells that, the proportional solitary wave solution of a decoupled BBM system is generally not stable, unless one component is 00. Indeed, if the solitary wave (ϕω,ψω)(\phi_{\omega},\psi_{\omega}) is perturbed in such a way that the initial data are exactly a new pair of solitary waves (ϕω1,ψω2)(\phi_{\omega_{1}},\psi_{\omega_{2}}) that are close to (ϕω,ψω)(\phi_{\omega},\psi_{\omega}), but ω1≠ω2\omega_{1}\neq\omega_{2}, then the solution (new pair of solitary waves) will slip away form (ϕω,ψω)(\phi_{\omega},\psi_{\omega}) as time goes on, hence not stable according to the definition we are using here. This seems due to the proportional requirements. This conclusion more or less goes against intuition. The fact that each component is stable while the combination is unstable actually brings up interesting questions: does there exist coupled non-proportional solitary wave solutions and if so, are they stable? Is there a different definition of stability that can accommodate the missing stability that solely caused by the phase difference?

In the study of vector solitons in birefringent nonlinear optical fibers, the nonlinear Schro¨\ddot{o}dinger equations have been proved numerically to have non-proportional solitary wave solution [19]. Next, the authors hope to investigate the similar subject in other dispersive equation system such as coupled BBM model.

The final example is an analogy to the one in [19] for a coupled nonlinear Scho¨\ddot{o}rdinger equations.

ut+ux−ux​x​t+((u2+β​v2)​u)x=0,u_{t}+u_{x}-u_{xxt}+((u^{2}+\beta v^{2})u)_{x}=0,

If β=1\beta=1, then det(ℳ)=13=1p+1\det(\mathcal{M})={1\over 3}={1\over p+1}.
If β≠1,μ=0\beta\neq 1,\mu=0, then det(ℳ)=β3<1p+1⇒β<1\det(\mathcal{M})={\beta\over 3}<{1\over p+1}\Rightarrow\beta<1.
If β≠1,μ≠0\beta\neq 1,\mu\neq 0, then μ2=1,det(ℳ)<13⇒β2>1\mu^{2}=1,\det(\mathcal{M})<{1\over 3}\Rightarrow\beta^{2}>1.
